newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir relief crew fits spacechairs at Baikonur.
newsitem.headline: Mir relief crew fits spacechairs at Baikonur.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts due to relieve the weary crew of the crippled Mir space station spent Wednesday adjusting chairs on the spacecraft that will take them into orbit on August 5, Interfax news agency said.

The new commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov were making the preparations at the launch pad in Baikonur, the cosmodrome that Russia rents from neighbouring Kazakhstan, Interfax said.

Meanwhile the three men currently aboard Mir have returned to routine work after last week's computer crash and were carrying out experiments and working on technical documents, a Mission Control spokeswoman told Reuters.

Their replacements are due to perform daring spacewalks inside and outside the stricken Mir to repair its electricity system and probably seal a puncture made during a manoeuvre accident on June 25, the worst in Mir's 11-year history.

Solovyov and Vinogradov will travel back to the Cosmonauts' Training Centre near Moscow after they have finished inspecting the Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft. The Soyuz-5 booster rocket will be delivered to Baikonur on Wednesday or Thursday and the spacecraft will be connected to the booster on August 1 or 2.

In the remaining days before the launch the pair will have to simulate manual docking with the station, Interfax said. The docking, scheduled for August 7, is due to be carried out in automatic mode but cosmonauts have to be prepared for manual operations in case of any malfunction.
The Mission Control spokeswoman, who could not confirm the whereabouts of the relief crew, said the three men on board Mir had only routine work scheduled for Wednesday.

"Thank God, they returned to a scheduled routine. They are conducting experiments in their beloved greenhouse, and the two Russian cosmonauts are doing physical exercises needed for their return to Earth," she said.
"(NASA astronaut Michael) Foale is studying human sleep in space conditions," she added.

Interfax news agency quoted a senior space official as saying the crew would soon try to crank up some of the gyroscopic devices, which were still not working after last week's computer crash, caused by a human error.
Earlier this week the crew fixed eight of the station's 12 gyrodine devices, which keep Mir's solar panels lined up to the Sun and are vital for steady orientation.
The spokeswoman said eight gyrodines were enough for Mir's stability in orbit and that repairs to the remaining devices were not in the immediate plans.
Interfax said commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, guided by Mission Control experts form the Earth, expected to fix two devices in the coming two days.

Tsibliyev, who developed heart trouble after the accident, and Lazutkin will keep Mir ticking over in orbit until they hand over to the replacements in about two weeks. They will fly home aboard a Soyuz two weeks ahead of schedule on August 14.
NASA physicist Foale will stay on board until a U.S. shuttle arrives on September 20.
